overview.subtitle: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar. It is a month of fasting from dawn to sunset, focused worship, Quran recitation, community care, and spiritual renewal.
body: The Quran describes Ramadan as the month in which the Quran was revealed as guidance for humanity. Muslims fast to develop taqwa (God-consciousness), discipline their desires, and increase empathy for those in need.
Beyond fasting, Ramadan is a time to elevate worship through prayer, charity, and reflection. Families gather, communities host iftars, and masajid become centers of learning and service.
Every day in Ramadan is an invitation to reset habits, strengthen spiritual focus, and renew intentions with sincerity.
key_points: Fasting is an act of worship and self-discipline.
Ramadan is the month in which the Quran was revealed.
The last ten nights are especially blessed, including Laylat al-Qadr.
Charity and community care are central to the month.
Every day is an opportunity to improve character and habits.

history.subtitle: Ramadan is linked to the Quranic revelation and the obligation of fasting. Its devotional rhythm has shaped Muslim worship, ethics, and communal life for centuries.
body: The Quran frames fasting in Ramadan as a prescribed act for believers and ties the month to revelation and guidance.
Prophetic practice established suhoor, iftar at sunset, and intensified night worship, while the last ten nights emphasize Laylat al-Qadr and spiritual retreat (i'tikaf).
Across centuries, Ramadan shaped daily routines, public worship, and charitable life, anchored by mosques, learning circles, and family gatherings.
Modern Ramadan carries these traditions worldwide through organized charity, community programming, and digital learning.

timeline.detail: First Quranic revelation occurs in Ramadan, traditionally associated with Laylat al-Qadr.
Fasting in Ramadan is prescribed for believers (Qur'an 2:183-185).
Ramadan practices consolidate within the early Muslim community, emphasizing communal prayer and charity.
Ramadan observance spreads across expanding Muslim communities in the Middle East, North Africa, and Asia.
Legal and devotional scholarship elaborates fasting practice, moon sighting, and community observance.
Regional traditions develop in Andalusia, the Maghreb, Egypt, and the Levant alongside urban mosque life.
Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal societies expand public iftars, endowments, and Quran education.
Global Ramadan programming, large-scale iftars, and coordinated charity expand community impact.
Ramadan continues to unite communities worldwide through worship, service, and family ties.

how_to_fast.intro: Fasting is from dawn to sunset with the intention (niyyah). The goal is worship, discipline, and avoiding what breaks the fast.

cards.title: Do's
items: Eat a balanced Suhoor and hydrate well.
Pray on time and read Quran daily.
Break fast promptly at sunset with dates and water if possible.
Be mindful of behavior, speech, and time.
Make dua before Iftar - it is a special time for acceptance.

cards.title: Don'ts
items: Do not eat or drink between Fajr and Maghrib.
Avoid backbiting, arguments, and harmful speech.
Do not neglect prayers or Quran.
Avoid wasting time in unhelpful activities.

charity_guide.intro: Charity is central in Ramadan. Zakat al-Fitr is obligatory before Eid prayer, while ongoing sadaqah builds compassion.
overview: Zakat al-Fitr purifies the fasting person from minor shortcomings and ensures everyone can celebrate Eid with dignity.
Sadaqah is voluntary charity given throughout the month. Even small, consistent giving can have a large impact.

items.question: When does Ramadan 2026 start?
items.answer: Most North American calendars project the first fast on February 17, 2026, with the first Taraweeh night on February 16, 2026. Local moon sighting can shift this by a day, so confirm with your local masjid.

items.question: What time does the daily fast begin and end?
items.answer: Fasting is from true dawn (Fajr) until sunset (Maghrib). Follow your local prayer timetable for your exact city times.

items.question: Who is exempt from fasting?
items.answer: Children before puberty, the ill, travelers, pregnant or nursing women, and those menstruating are exempt. Missed fasts are made up later when possible; ask a local scholar about fidya or kaffarah in your situation.

items.question: What breaks the fast?
items.answer: Eating or drinking, sexual relations, intentional vomiting, and menstrual or postpartum bleeding break the fast. If you eat or drink out of forgetfulness, the fast remains valid according to most Sunni opinions.

items.question: How can I make the most of the last 10 nights?
items.answer: Prioritize night prayer, Quran, dua, and charity, and focus on the odd nights (21, 23, 25, 27, 29) for Laylat al-Qadr. Many people adjust sleep schedules or take time off to focus on worship.
